# Blind re-identification: can you tell who is across the net?

*Generated by `experiments/blind_reid/run.py`. The unit is one **performance** — a single player in a single match — vectorized from the decoded notation with the name stripped. Scores are **verification AUC** (the chance a same-player pair is closer than a different-player pair; 0.5 = chance) and **rank-1 accuracy** (is a performance's nearest neighbour the same player), each computed only on players held out of the distance metric's fit.*

- **Men:** 7,477 performances, 995 players (capped at 30 per player); metric fit on 3,677, scored on 3,800 from 497 held-out players.
- **Women:** 5,529 performances, 727 players (capped at 30 per player); metric fit on 2,706, scored on 2,823 from 363 held-out players.

## Headline: yes, and the serve is not how

| block | features | AUC (men) | AUC (women) | rank-1 (men) | chance | rank-1 (women) | chance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **serve** | 10 | 0.643 | 0.642 | 0.044 | 0.0055 | 0.043 | 0.0069 |
| **return** | 7 | 0.617 | 0.611 | 0.037 | 0.0055 | 0.041 | 0.0069 |
| **rally** | 11 | 0.677 | 0.666 | 0.058 | 0.0055 | 0.058 | 0.0069 |
| **response** | 18 | 0.685 | 0.672 | 0.109 | 0.0055 | 0.082 | 0.0069 |
| **all** | 28 | 0.713 | 0.702 | 0.171 | 0.0055 | 0.132 | 0.0069 |

Shuffling the identity labels collapses every block to chance (null AUC 0.497 men, 0.503 women), so the machinery is not leaking.

![blocks](figures/blind_reid_blocks.png)

The **response** block — returns plus rally strokes, nothing about the delivery — beats the **serve** block outright (0.685 vs 0.643 for the men, 0.672 vs 0.642 for the women), and the rally strokes alone are enough to do it (0.677 men from 11 features). So the intuition that you would name your opponent from their serve is backwards: the serve is the *weakest* of the three views. What gives a player away is what comes back once the point is live.

Rank-1 accuracy on the response block is 0.109 against a chance rate of 0.0055 — 20x chance, from one match, with the serve withheld and against a gallery of every other held-out performance.

## Which single measurements carry identity

Single-feature AUC (men), top 10 and bottom 5:

| feature | block | AUC |
|---|---|---|
| `ral_net` | response | 0.613 |
| `ret_slice` | response | 0.610 |
| `ral_slice` | response | 0.596 |
| `net_point_rate` | response | 0.588 |
| `ral_fh` | response | 0.575 |
| `avg_rally_len` | response | 0.574 |
| `sv_ace` | serve | 0.572 |
| `shots_per_point` | response | 0.567 |
| `sv_deuce_wide` | serve | 0.567 |
| `ral_unforced` | response | 0.567 |
| … | | |
| `ret_dir3` | response | 0.531 |
| `sv_df` | serve | 0.531 |
| `ral_dir3` | response | 0.519 |
| `ret_fh` | response | 0.518 |
| `ret_in` | response | 0.516 |

All six of the most identifying single features are response features. Net-play rate, slice reliance (on the return and in the rally), forehand share and rally tempo are the fingerprint. Serve *direction* is close to noise at this resolution, and only ace rate ranks near the top of the serve block. Court-zone directions (`ral_dir3`, `ret_dir3`, `ret_fh`) are the weakest features of all: they say more about where the ball ended up than about who chose to hit it there.

## The controls

Each row is the same pair list, filtered — the question is whether the signal is the player or something correlated with the player.

| pairs restricted to | AUC (men) | AUC (women) | same-player pairs |
|---|---|---|---|
| all pairs | 0.685 | 0.672 | 37,900 |
| different charter | 0.672 | 0.666 | 26,340 |
| same charter | 0.691 | 0.665 | 11,560 |
| different opponent | 0.682 | 0.671 | 36,717 |
| same handedness | 0.673 | 0.671 | 37,688 |
| different surface | 0.672 | 0.668 | 17,946 |
| 3+ years apart | 0.673 | 0.659 | 16,192 |
| 6+ years apart | 0.678 | 0.650 | 5,495 |
| strict: charter + opponent + surface all differ | 0.663 | 0.666 | 12,493 |

![controls](figures/blind_reid_controls.png)

The signal is not an artefact. Forcing every pair to differ in charter, opponent **and** surface at once costs about two points of AUC (0.685 → 0.663 for the men). The charter deserves its own check, since notation habits could easily masquerade as player habits: asking the same vectors to identify the **charter** instead of the player gives AUC 0.538 (0.534 restricted to different-player pairs), barely above chance. Conditioning every rate on charted denominators (see `features.py`) is what buys that.

Handedness contributes a little but is nowhere near the whole story: restricting to same-handed pairs, where lefty-vs-righty can no longer help, costs 0.011 AUC.

## Are players more like each other than like their past selves?

This was the question the experiment was built for. The answer is mostly no: players are their own nearest kind, and clearly so.

- **Men:** of 162 held-out players with 6+ scored performances, **2** (1%) sit further from their own other showings than from the field's. Median own-spread 4.89 vs 5.75 to the field.
- **Women:** of 132 held-out players with 6+ scored performances, **7** (5%) sit further from their own other showings than from the field's. Median own-spread 4.98 vs 5.67 to the field.

![distances](figures/blind_reid_distances.png)

Time does erode it, though, and by a measurable amount. Scored inside each gap band, men's AUC falls from 0.670 for pairs from the same season to 0.620 at six to nine years apart, which is roughly a third of the lift above chance. So a player is still clearly recognisable years later, just less reliably. That lines up with `career_splits` rather than cutting against it: styles really do drift, and this puts a rate on it.

![drift](figures/blind_reid_drift.png)

That figure is scored with AUC rather than with a distance, and the reason is worth stating because the distance version misleads. A player's raw distance to their own older performances does grow with the year gap (men: 4.73 at no gap to 5.17 at ten years and up), which looks like decay. But two things move between bins. Performances from distant eras sit further apart whoever hit them, so the different-player median shifts as well, and the spread of the distribution changes, so a fixed gap in raw units does not mean the same thing in every bin. AUC is rank-based and pits same-player pairs against different-player pairs *from the same bin*, so it is immune to both:

| years apart | AUC (men) | AUC (women) | men: same-player median | men: different-player median | men: same-player pairs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.670 | 0.683 | 4.73 | 5.60 | 6,392 |
| 1–2 | 0.652 | 0.654 | 4.89 | 5.66 | 15,316 |
| 3–5 | 0.629 | 0.638 | 5.02 | 5.68 | 10,697 |
| 6–9 | 0.620 | 0.613 | 5.12 | 5.69 | 4,267 |
| 10+ | 0.683 | 0.638 | 5.17 | 6.23 | 1,228 |

Two things in that table need flagging. The **10+ band rebounds** (men 0.683), and that is not a recovery of identity: it rests on 1,228 same-player pairs, it can only contain players charted across a decade or more, and its different-player median jumps to 6.23, so era separation is helping tell strangers apart too.

And the **cumulative year-gap rows in the controls table above are flattered** by the same effect. "6+ years apart" reads 0.678 there, well above the 0.620 of the six-to-nine band, because pooling six-to-nine with ten-plus mixes two distance scales and lets same-player pairs from the tighter band beat different-player pairs from the wider one. The per-band numbers are the ones to trust; the cumulative rows are kept because they are the natural first thing to compute and it is worth showing why they mislead.

Still, the crossings exist. Pairs of **different** players whose performances sit closer to each other than to either player's own other showings (men, response block):

| player A | player B | cross-distance | A's own | B's own |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jason Kubler | Pedro Cachin | 4.11 | 5.01 | 4.42 |
| Hyeon Chung | Jason Kubler | 4.75 | 4.96 | 5.01 |
| Jason Kubler | Kamil Majchrzak | 4.41 | 5.01 | 4.61 |
| Jason Kubler | Karue Sell | 4.58 | 5.01 | 4.72 |
| Cristian Garin | Jason Kubler | 4.58 | 4.71 | 5.01 |
| Borna Coric | Jason Kubler | 4.46 | 4.56 | 5.01 |
| Francisco Comesana | Max Purcell | 6.09 | 6.17 | 6.46 |
| Egor Gerasimov | Jason Kubler | 3.95 | 4.03 | 5.01 |
| Jason Kubler | Nuno Borges | 4.94 | 5.01 | 5.15 |
| Jason Kubler | Taylor Fritz | 4.94 | 5.01 | 5.11 |

Note how often one name recurs: **Jason Kubler** appears in 9 of the 10 listed pairs. The bar is the smaller of the two self-distances, so these are genuinely mutual, but a player with a wide own cloud will naturally cross with more of the field. Read it as style fluidity rather than as a resemblance to any one opponent.

Tightest own clouds relative to the field (men), the most self-identical players:

|---|---|---|---|

## What limits the accuracy

Not the weakness of the fingerprint, but the size of the sample. Splitting held-out performances into quartiles by charted points, men's rank-1 rises from 0.050 in the shortest quarter of matches to 0.125 in the longest. The women's series is noisier and not monotone (0.054, 0.058, 0.093, 0.080), so the size effect is clear for the men and only directional for the women:

| quartile | charted points | rank-1 (men) | rank-1 (women) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 | 64–118 | 0.050 | 0.054 |
| Q2 | 119–157 | 0.081 | 0.058 |
| Q3 | 158–207 | 0.081 | 0.093 |
| Q4 | 208–980 | 0.125 | 0.080 |

![size](figures/blind_reid_size.png)

A rate estimated from a 90-point match is mostly sampling noise; the same rate over a five-setter is a measurement. The identity is presumably there in both, and we can just read it better in the long one.

## Caveats

- **Style, not identity.** A high AUC does not mean these features name a human; it means they narrow the field. Two players with genuinely similar games stay confusable no matter how much data we add.
- **Opponent reactivity.** What a player hits back is partly the opponent's doing. The different-opponent control shows this is not the main driver, but `avg_rally_len` in particular is a property of the *match* (both players share it), kept because rally tempo is also a real trait and dropped pairs from the same match make it non-circular.
- **Era mixes with identity.** The field spans 1960–2026 and pre-1990 matches are sparse, differently charted, and stylistically distant. Some players with wide own-spread (Guillermo Vilas is the extreme: own spread far above the field median, on six performances across 1977–1986 and two surfaces) are being measured across an era gap, not caught being inconsistent.
- **Charting coverage skew.** Inherited from the whole repo: later rounds and bigger names are charted more, so the player mix is not the tour's.
- **Distances are not comparable across year-gap bands.** Both the level and the spread of the distance distribution shift with the era gap, which is why the drift analysis is scored with AUC inside each band and why the cumulative year-gap controls read high. Any future cut along a dimension that moves the distance scale needs the same treatment.
- **Serve resolution.** The serve block is limited to direction, in-rate and outcome. Real serve identification would use speed, spin and toss, none of which the notation records — so "the serve is the weakest block" is a statement about *charted* serve data, not about serves.
